# Dartmoor National Park

Scroll down


## A land of contrasts

**Wild, open moorlands and deep river valleys, with a rich history and rare wildlife, striking tors and swathes of heather, Dartmoor will touch your soul.**

With 450 miles of paths to walk, cycle, run or ride, thousands of archaeological sites and features to discover the past, Dartmoor is packed full of stunning views that steal your breath, mysterious stories to intrigue and spaces to simply sit and be.

- [@dartmoornpa](https://twitter.com/@dartmoornpa)
- [enjoydartmoor1](https://facebook.com/enjoydartmoor1)

## Key activities

Visiting one of our three Visitor Centres is a great way to start your visit. Find out more about a variety of activities suitable for families, couples or groups and plan what you’d like to see and do.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/NT_180513_0362-lr-600x400.jpg)

Activity

### Exploring , Activity

Follow one of the many routes such as the Dartmoor Way or Wray Valley Trail on foot or by bike. Or maybe take a compass and a map to explore the moor in your own way.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Creamtea-KT-DNPA-2015-25-600x400.jpg)

Activity

### Eating & Drinking , Activity

What can be more rewarding after a long (or short!) walk than visiting one of Dartmoor’s pubs, restaurants or tea houses. Whether you prefer gourmet food or a cream tea, there are plenty of choices.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/20180822-DNPA-SJ-MeldonWildlifeFestival-71-600x400.jpg)

Activity

### Discovering , Activity

Dip into Dartmoor’s incredible history, find out more about its rare wildlife and special habitats. Come along to one of our many events or discover for yourself.

![Special qualities](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/2012-DNPA-Drizzlecombe_Stonerow-1920x1080.jpg)

## Special qualities

Overview

“I have never before, in my long and eclectic career, been gifted with such an abundance of natural beauty as I experienced filming War Horse on Dartmoor.” Steven Spielberg.

Dartmoor’s granite tors, rich coloured rivers and open landscapes have inspired authors, poets and artists for years. From Arthur Conan Doyle’s Sherlock Holmes, Agatha Christie’s detective Poirot and the evocative works of Widgery to the contemporary folk songs of Seth Lakeman.

Steeped in history Dartmoor is the most important site for Bronze Age archaeology in western Europe, it’s home to the Dartmoor pony which can be seen grazing wild with foals close by and it’s the only place in the world where you can find the tiny Bog Hoverfly. In Dartmoor’s woodlands you might spot the world’s largest land slug the whopping Black Ash Slug that can exceed 20cm!

Find a river side spot for a picnic, walk Stallmoor stone row – the longest in the world, explore a hut circle and cross a clapper bridge or climb a tor and take in the natural beauty of Dartmoor, it will leave you uplifted, refreshed and revived.

## Did you know?

Dartmoor National Park is a vast moorland in the county of Devon. Dartmoor ponies roam its craggy landscape, defined by forests, rivers, wetlands and granite tors created about 280 million years ago. Trails wind through valleys with Neolithic tombs, Bronze Age stone circles and abandoned medieval farmhouses. The area is dotted with villages, including Princetown, home to Dartmoor Prison used during the Napoleonic Wars.

# **Enjoying Dartmoor**

Dartmoor doesn’t just have places, it has special places. These are places that are set apart from the ordinary or the mundane. This could be due to their history, their setting, their offer or often due to all of this and more.

Start your journey in one of Dartmoor’s towns or villages and discover what makes them so special. Maybe it’s because they’re a market town, a Medieval Stannary town or just a great place to start a walk or ride from. What you can be sure of is the welcome and the quality of the food and drink.

Venturing further up on to the Moor, come and discover one of three National Park Visitor Centres. With a wealth of natural and built beauty, opportunities for short or long walks and things to do for people of all ages, they make great bases to explore Dartmoor.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/20171126-DNPA-SJ-Ella-and-Lucas-Sharpitor-19-1920x1080.jpg)

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Granitegears-Cycling-LeePengelly-DNPA-2014-32-580x580.jpg)

### Getting around

Dartmoor can be explored on foot, bike, horse or vehicle. There are several bus services running from the main moorland towns and for hassle free travel there are organised trips with a variety of coach companies.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/NT_180513_1029-lr-580x580.jpg)

### Getting there

Dartmoor National Park has train stations nearby in Exeter, Newton Abbot, Totnes, Ivybridge and Plymouth. The average journey time from London is 4 hours.

Exeter Airport offers access from the rest of the UK and internationally.

There are good road links to the gateway moorland towns.

View down the River Meavy towards Leather Tor and Sharpitor | | [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/Dartmoor_National_Park_UK_location_map.svg/330px-Dartmoor_National_Park_UK_location_map.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dartmoor_National_Park_UK_location_map.svg) | | Location | [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") ( [South West England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_West_England "South West England")) | | Coordinates | [50°34′N4°0′W﻿ / ﻿50.567°N 4.000°W﻿ / 50.567; -4.000](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Dartmoor¶ms=50_34_N_4_0_W_type:landmark_dim:32km) | | Area | 954km2 (368sqmi) | | Established | 1951 | | Visitors | 10.98m | | Governingbody | Dartmoor National Park Authority | | Website | [www.dartmoor.gov.uk](https://www.dartmoor.gov.uk/) | **Dartmoor** is an [upland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highland "Highland") area in southern [Devon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devon "Devon"), [South West England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_West_England "South West England"). The [moorland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorland "Moorland") and surrounding land has been protected by [National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks_of_the_United_Kingdom "National parks of the United Kingdom") status since 1951. **Dartmoor National Park** covers 954km2 (368sqmi).[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmoor_National_Park#cite_note-DF-1) The [granite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granite "Granite") that forms the uplands dates from the [Carboniferous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carboniferous "Carboniferous") Period of geological history. The landscape consists of moorland capped with many exposed granite hilltops known as [tors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tor_(rock_formation) "Tor (rock formation)"), providing habitats for wildlife. The highest point is [High Willhays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Willhays "High Willhays"), 621m (2,037ft) above sea level. The entire area is rich in antiquities and archaeological [artefacts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artifact_(archaeology) "Artifact (archaeology)"). Dartmoor National Park is managed by the [Dartmoor National Park Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmoor_National_Park_Authority "Dartmoor National Park Authority"), whose 22 members are drawn from [Devon County Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devon_County_Council "Devon County Council"), local [district councils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Districts_of_England "Districts of England") and Government. The [Dartmoor Commoners' Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmoor_Commoners'_Council "Dartmoor Commoners' Council") exists to create and enforce regulations regarding commoners' rights. [Parts of Dartmoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmoor_Training_Area "Dartmoor Training Area") have been used as military [firing ranges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firing_range "Firing range") for over 200 years. The public is granted extensive land access rights on Dartmoor (including restricted access to the firing ranges) and it is a popular tourist destination. ## Physical geography \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dartmoor&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Physical geography")\] ### Geology \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dartmoor&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Geology")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Cornubian_batholith.png/500px-Cornubian_batholith.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cornubian_batholith.png) Map showing the main granite outcrops of the [Cornubian batholith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornubian_batholith "Cornubian batholith") in southwest England and the gravity anomaly associated with it Main article: [Geology of Dartmoor National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_Dartmoor_National_Park "Geology of Dartmoor National Park") Dartmoor includes the largest area of [granite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granite "Granite") in Britain, with about 625km2 (241mi2) at the surface, though most of it is under superficial [peat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peat "Peat") deposits. The granite (or more specifically [adamellite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adamellite "Adamellite")) was intruded at depth as a [pluton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluton "Pluton") into the surrounding sedimentary rocks during the [Carboniferous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carboniferous "Carboniferous") period, probably about 309 million years ago.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmoor_National_Park#cite_note-2) It is generally accepted that the present surface is not far below the original top of the pluton; evidence for this includes partly digested [shale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shale "Shale") [xenoliths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xenolith "Xenolith"), contamination of the granite and the existence of two patches of altered [sedimentary rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedimentary_rock "Sedimentary rock") on top of the granite.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmoor_National_Park#cite_note-3) A considerable [gravity anomaly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravity_anomaly "Gravity anomaly") is associated with the Dartmoor pluton as with [other such plutons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravity_anomalies_of_Britain_and_Ireland "Gravity anomalies of Britain and Ireland").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmoor_National_Park#cite_note-4) Measurement of the anomaly has helped to determine the likely shape and extent of the rock mass at depth. ### Tors \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dartmoor&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Tors")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/High_Willhays.jpg/250px-High_Willhays.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:High_Willhays.jpg) [High Willhays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Willhays "High Willhays") with Yes Tor behind Dartmoor is known for its [tors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tor_(rock_formation) "Tor (rock formation)") – hills topped with outcrops of bedrock, which in [granite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granite "Granite") country such as this are usually rounded boulder-like formations. Each tor represents a mass of granite left standing where deep chemical weathering removed the surrounding, more heavily jointed rock. More than 160 of the hills of Dartmoor have the word _tor_ in their name but quite a number do not.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmoor_National_Park#cite_note-DF-1) However, this does not appear to relate to whether or not there is an outcrop of rock on their summit. The tors are the focus of an annual event known as the [Ten Tors Challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ten_Tors_Challenge "Ten Tors Challenge"), when around 2,400 people aged between 14 and 19 walk for distances of 35, 45 or 55mi (56, 72 or 89km) between ten tors on many different routes. The highest points on Dartmoor are on the northern moor: [High Willhays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Willhays "High Willhays"), 621m (2,037ft), ( [grid reference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Survey_National_Grid "Ordnance Survey National Grid") [SX 580892](http://streetmap.co.uk/grid/258000_89200_115)) and [Yes Tor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_Tor "Yes Tor"), 619m (2,031ft), ( [grid reference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Survey_National_Grid "Ordnance Survey National Grid") [SX 581901](http://streetmap.co.uk/grid/258100_90100_115)). The highest points on the southern moor are [Ryder's Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryder's_Hill "Ryder's Hill"), 515m (1,690ft), ( [grid reference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Survey_National_Grid "Ordnance Survey National Grid") [SX 660690](http://streetmap.co.uk/grid/266000_69000_115)), Snowdon 495m (1,624ft), ( [grid reference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Survey_National_Grid "Ordnance Survey National Grid") [SX 668684](http://streetmap.co.uk/grid/266800_68400_115)), and an unnamed point, 493m (1,617ft) at ( [grid reference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Survey_National_Grid "Ordnance Survey National Grid") [SX 603645](http://streetmap.co.uk/grid/260300_64500_115)), between Langcombe Hill and Shell Top. The best-known tor on Dartmoor is [Haytor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haytor "Haytor")[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmoor_National_Park#cite_note-5) (called Hey Tor by William Crossing), 457m (1,499ft), ( [grid reference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Survey_National_Grid "Ordnance Survey National Grid") [SX 757771](http://streetmap.co.uk/grid/275700_77100_115)). For a more complete list see [List of Dartmoor tors and hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Dartmoor_tors_and_hills "List of Dartmoor tors and hills"). ### Rivers \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dartmoor&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Rivers")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/ErmeIvybridge.jpg/250px-ErmeIvybridge.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ErmeIvybridge.jpg) [River Erme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Erme "River Erme") at [Ivybridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivybridge "Ivybridge") The high ground of Dartmoor forms the [catchment area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drainage_basin "Drainage basin") for many of Devon's rivers. As well as shaping the landscape, these have traditionally provided a source of power for moor industries such as [tin mining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmoor_tin-mining "Dartmoor tin-mining") and quarrying. The moor takes its name from the [River Dart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Dart "River Dart"), which starts as the [East Dart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Dart "East Dart") and [West Dart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Dart "West Dart") and then becomes a single river at [Dartmeet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmeet "Dartmeet"). It leaves the moor at [Buckfastleigh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckfastleigh "Buckfastleigh"), flowing through [Totnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Totnes "Totnes") below where it opens up into a long [ria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ria "Ria"), reaching the sea at [Dartmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth,_Devon "Dartmouth, Devon"). Other rivers flowing from Dartmoor include the [Teign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teign "Teign"), the [Taw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Taw "River Taw"), the [Tavy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tavy "Tavy"), the [Avon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Avon,_Devon "River Avon, Devon"), and the [Lyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Lyd,_Devon "River Lyd, Devon"). Some of the rivers in Dartmoor have been dammed to create [reservoirs for drinking water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmoor_reservoirs "Dartmoor reservoirs"), including the River Avon[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmoor_National_Park#cite_note-6) and the South Teign River (Fernworthy Reservoir).[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmoor_National_Park#cite_note-7) ### Bogs \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dartmoor&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Bogs")\] Much more rain falls on Dartmoor than in the surrounding lowlands. As much of the national park is covered in thick layers of [peat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peat "Peat") (decaying vegetation), the rain is usually absorbed quickly and distributed slowly, so the moor is rarely dry. In areas where water accumulates, dangerous [bogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bog "Bog") or mires can result. Some of these, topped with bright green moss, are known to locals as "feather beds" or "quakers", because they can shift (or 'quake') beneath a person's feet. Quakers result from sphagnum moss growing over the water that accumulates in the hollows in the granite.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmoor_National_Park#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmoor_National_Park#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmoor_National_Park#cite_note-10) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Aune_head_mire3.jpg/250px-Aune_head_mire3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aune_head_mire3.jpg) [Aune Mire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aune_Mire?action=edit&redlink=1 "Aune Mire (page does not exist)"), the source of the [River Avon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Avon,_Devon "River Avon, Devon") The vegetation of the bogs depends on the type and location. [Blanket bog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanket_bog "Blanket bog"), which forms on the highest land where the rainfall exceeds 2,000 millimetres (79in) a year, consists mainly of cotton-grass ( _[eriophorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eriophorum "Eriophorum")_ species), sedges ( _[carex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carex "Carex")_ and _[rhynchospora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhynchospora "Rhynchospora")_), _[Bog Asphodel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bog_Asphodel "Bog Asphodel")_ and _[Common Tormentil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Tormentil "Common Tormentil")_, with _[sphagnum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphagnum "Sphagnum")_ thriving in the wettest patches.
